title: Kim et al. (2015) True/False Quiz
instructions: Choose True or False, then use the explanation to distinguish beliefs, support behaviors, living arrangements, and emotional ties. Keep each study's population, historical context, and limits on causal interpretation in view.

items.prompt: In the study of undergraduates in Beijing, a larger proportion endorsed providing financial support to parents as necessary for adulthood than endorsed being able to support their own children.
items.explanation: Among students at Beijing Normal University, 89% endorsed financial support to parents and 86% endorsed being able to support their own children. These percentages describe criteria for adulthood in the cited study, not rates of actual support provision.
items.source: The paradox of filial norms and behavior

items.prompt: Western norms of filial responsibility also include living near older parents, caring for them when sick, providing financial help when needed, and maintaining regular contact.
items.explanation: The chapter recognizes obligations to assist parents in Western societies. It distinguishes filial piety by its emphasis on respect, obedience, and saving parents' face, as well as lifelong responsibility even when parents do not need help.

items.prompt: The figures of 33% seeing parents only once a year and 12% not visiting for many years were measured in the same sample as the 89% of Beijing undergraduates, demonstrating contradictions within those individuals.
items.explanation: The adulthood criteria and visiting frequencies came from different studies cited in the chapter. They illustrate a broader tension between norms and behavior, but do not pair the same individuals' attitudes with their actions.

items.prompt: In the Dual Filial Piety Model (DFPM), reciprocal filial piety involves support motivated by love, gratitude, and repayment for parents' sacrifices and long-term investment.
items.explanation: Reciprocal filial piety emphasizes willingness to express love and care, grounded in gratitude for parental investment. It differs from obedience based on parental authority.

items.prompt: High normative solidarity means, by definition, that functional solidarity through actual financial and care exchanges must also be high.
items.explanation: Normative solidarity concerns beliefs about obligations to assist parents. Functional solidarity concerns actual exchanges. These are distinct dimensions, so one cannot automatically be inferred from the other.

items.prompt: Authoritarian filial piety is a voluntary norm that applies only when parents need practical help, like the need-based account of Western filial responsibility.
items.explanation: Authoritarian filial piety emphasizes parents' absolute authority, hierarchy, suppression of one's own wishes, and obedience based on one's role as an offspring. It is not defined as voluntary assistance restricted to parental need.

items.prompt: The comparison of mainland China and Taiwan using 1990s data illustrates why economic development alone cannot explain the direction of change in filial piety.
items.explanation: Taiwan was more economically developed at the time but more traditional on some beliefs, including coresidence after marriage and daughters-in-law as primary caregivers. The chapter also discusses government approaches to Confucian values and the role of family-based businesses.

items.prompt: In changing social contexts, adult children who cannot provide hands-on care may express filial piety by paying for high-quality professional institutional care.
items.explanation: The chapter cites research in China describing a shift from stigmatizing institutional care to reinterpreting it as filial provision when direct care is unavailable. Such costly practices may be specific to particular social classes.

items.prompt: The chapter concludes that China's Family Support Agreements and long-term care insurance in Japan and South Korea preserve filial piety unchanged, without affecting spontaneity or the division of support roles.
items.explanation: Governments have stepped in to fill support gaps, with long-term care insurance introduced in Japan in 2000 and South Korea in 2008. The chapter raises possible unintended erosion of filial support; legal sanctions in Family Support Agreements may reduce spontaneity, flexibility, affection, and trust. These are possibilities, not established universal effects.

items.prompt: The coresidence rates cited in the chapter—14% in the United States, 43% in Japan, and 68.7% in China—can by themselves directly rank filial piety and care quality across the three countries.
items.explanation: The percentages come from different cited national studies and are not current rates measured in a common survey. Coresidence does not automatically ensure good care or relationships, and living apart does not rule out support exchanges. It is not a single cultural score for filial piety.

items.prompt: Quasi-coresidence means parents and children maintain separate households nearby, balancing opportunities for support with independence.
items.explanation: Examples include living in the same village or community, or in neighboring houses, while maintaining separate households. Physical proximity does not guarantee frequent interaction or better well-being, as the cited Korean findings caution.

items.prompt: Intergenerational coresidence in Asia is determined only by older parents' health needs; adult children's housing and childcare needs are irrelevant.
items.explanation: Parental health decline and widowhood can prompt coresidence, but so can children's housing costs, marriage, and childcare needs. The chapter describes mutual aid shaped by both generations' needs and resources.

items.prompt: Research cited in the chapter found that adult children who migrated to urban areas for work tended to send parents more money than non-migrant children, compensating for the absence of hands-on care.
items.explanation: Living apart can constrain help with daily activities without eliminating financial exchanges. The cited migration study describes greater financial provision as compensation for unavailable direct care, rather than treating distance as the absence of support.

items.prompt: Intergenerational ambivalence refers to experiencing positive and negative sentiments simultaneously about the same parent-child relationship.
items.explanation: The chapter discusses ambivalence at two levels: structural or sociological contradictions between role expectations, and subjective or psychological mixed feelings within a relationship.

items.prompt: If parents receiving more support have lower well-being in a cross-sectional study, this establishes that support from children caused their well-being to decline.
items.explanation: Parents with health problems may draw more help from their children. If the study cannot distinguish needs that prompt support from outcomes of support, an association with lower well-being can be mistaken for a harmful causal effect.
items.source: Reverse causation in support and well-being
